1163.title: Nyaya (logic)
1163.hook: the Nyaya Sutra sorts every argument into three kinds of talk, and only one of them is looking for the truth
1163.howItsDone: In traditional Sanskrit learning, Nyaya students practice vada, structured discussion with a teacher or fellow students, and formal debate, with each side setting out its reasons step by step, has a place in the tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nyaya's argument in five parts, said out loud, with the example doing the real work: where's your pot? A new week begins.

Three arguments are going on at the same wedding. At one table, two old friends are working out whether a hard decision was right, and each keeps saying, wait, say that again, I think you've got a point. At the next table, two uncles are arguing politics, and neither one is listening; each is just waiting for a gap to land the next blow. And in the corner, somebody has no opinion of his own at all. He just pokes holes in whatever anyone else says. Same noise. Same raised hands. The Nyaya Sutra says these are three different things, and it gives each one a name.
screen: `THREE ARGUMENTS, ONE WEDDING.` → `SAME NOISE, DIFFERENT AIMS.` → `NYAYA NAMES ALL THREE.`

segments.voice: The first is vada: discussion. In the Nyaya Sutra, vada is talk where both sides use the real means of knowing, perception, inference and the rest, and set out their reasons in yesterday's five parts, without contradicting their own starting points. The point isn't to win. It's to find out. Later the Sutra says vada is the kind of talk you have with a teacher, a student or fellow seekers, people who aren't jealous of being right. The second is jalpa: wrangling. Same parts, but now the aim is victory, so it reaches for tricks: twisting a word into a meaning the speaker never intended, raising objections that only sound like objections. The third is vitanda: cavil. Wrangling with no position of your own. You defend nothing. You only knock down. So far, one good kind of talk and two bad ones. But the Sutra adds a turn. Jalpa and vitanda have a use: they guard a true conclusion the way a hedge of thorny branches guards a sprouting seed. When someone comes only to trample, you may need thorns. So Nyaya doesn't pretend hard argument never happens. It asks you to know which kind you're in, and to remember the hedge exists for the seed. The seed is the truth, and the garden is vada. At a kitchen table, that becomes a practical question, halfway through any argument: am I trying to find out, or trying to win?
screen: `VADA: TALK THAT WANTS TO FIND OUT.` · `JALPA: TALK THAT WANTS TO WIN.` · `VITANDA: ONLY KNOCKING DOWN.` · `THORNS THAT GUARD A SEED.` · then, large: `FIND OUT, OR WIN?`

segments.voice: Replay one recent disagreement, at home, at work or online, without rearguing it; just watch it, as if from the next table. Was it vada, jalpa or vitanda, for you and for the other person? Then find the one honest question your next sentence could have been, and if you pray, ask for a mind that wants the truth more than the win.
Nyaya. Today, its three kinds of talk: vada, discussion that seeks the truth; jalpa, wrangling to win; and vitanda, attacking with no position of your own.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. The thorns are there to guard the seed. See you tomorrow.

1164.title: Nyaya (logic)
1164.hook: a bank teller holds a note up to the light, and Nyaya teaches you to do the same with a reason
1164.howItsDone: Students of Nyaya learn the hetvabhasas, the kinds of false reason, as part of the Nyaya Sutra's teaching, and use them to test arguments in discussion with a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nyaya, three kinds of talk: vada wants to find out, jalpa wants to win, vitanda only knocks down, and thorns that guard a seed.

At the bank counter, a teller takes a large note and, before she counts it, does something quick and almost unconscious. She holds it up to the light. She isn't accusing anybody. She just knows some notes look exactly like money and aren't. The color is right, the size is right, the number in the corner is right, and there's nothing behind it. The Nyaya Sutra thinks reasons are like that. Some are real. Some only look like reasons. And it gives the look-alikes a name, so you can learn to hold them up to the light.
screen: `A NOTE HELD UP TO THE LIGHT.` → `LOOKS LIKE MONEY, ISN'T.` → `SOME REASONS ARE LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: The name is hetvabhasa. Hetu is the reason, the second of the five parts. On the ridge with the smoke, you brushed past this idea; today it gets its own day. Abhasa is a semblance, a thing that shines like something it isn't. So a hetvabhasa is a reason that only looks like one. The Nyaya Sutra lists five. Here are three, in everyday clothes. The wandering reason shows up where your conclusion is true, but also where it isn't, so it can't carry you anywhere. This restaurant must be good, because it's crowded. But crowds also gather where food is cheap, or new, or the only place open late. The contradicting reason turns around and proves the opposite of what you wanted. I can't be a beginner at this, because I keep making beginner's mistakes. And the reason that still needs proving stands in the same spot as the claim, as unproved as what it was meant to prove. This plan will work, because it's a good plan. The note looks fine, but there's nothing behind it. Nyaya didn't keep this list to score points in debate. In the Sutra's opening, getting free of false knowledge is tied to the highest good, and a false reason is one of the quietest ways false knowledge gets in. So the habit it asks for is simple, and a little humbling: hold your own reasons up to the light first, before anyone else's.
screen: `HETVABHASA: A LOOK-ALIKE REASON.` · `THE WANDERING REASON.` · `THE REASON THAT FLIPS ON YOU.` · `THE REASON THAT NEEDS PROVING TOO.` · then, large: `HOLD YOUR OWN UP TO THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've told yourself lately with a because in it, like I'm bad at this, because, and say the reason quietly. Turn it over: does it wander, does it flip, does it need proving as much as the thing it holds up? You don't have to fix it; just look, rest with the breath, and if you pray, offer the reason up to be seen by a clearer light than yours.
Nyaya. Today, its hetvabhasa: the reason that only looks like a reason, and the habit of checking your own first.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Some reasons are notes with nothing behind them. Go gently.

1165.title: Nyaya (logic)
1165.hook: a shape at dusk could be a post or a person, and Nyaya says that moment of not knowing is where its whole path begins
1165.howItsDone: In the Nyaya tradition, study of logic is understood as part of the path to liberation; students begin with the opening sutras of the Nyaya Sutra, which tie true knowledge to the highest good.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hetvabhasa: a reason that only looks like one. Today is the last day with Nyaya.
screen: `HOLD YOUR OWN UP TO THE LIGHT.` · `NYAYA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: It's getting dark on a country road. Up ahead, at the edge of a field, a tall, thin shape stands perfectly still. A wooden post? A person, waiting? You can see height, and that it's upright. But the detail that would settle it, a hand, a face, the grain of the wood, isn't there yet. For a few seconds, you simply don't know. Nyaya teachers use this very picture, the post or the person at dusk, for doubt. And they don't treat it as a failure of the mind. They treat it as a doorway.
screen: `A SHAPE AT DUSK.` → `A POST, OR A PERSON?` → `NOT KNOWING, AS A DOORWAY.`

segments.voice: The Nyaya Sutra names doubt, samshaya, among the things a seeker must understand. Doubt is a mind pulled between two possibilities, because it sees what they share and can't yet see what tells them apart. Vatsyayana, its early commentator, makes a quiet point: nobody inquires into what is completely unknown, or into what is already settled. Inquiry lives in between, in doubt. In the Sutra's opening list, doubt comes right after the means of knowing and the things to be known, ahead of the example, the parts of an argument and the conclusion. Doubt isn't a detour on the way to reasoning. It's what gets reasoning going. The post and the person share height and stillness; that's why you're stuck. So the way out isn't to stare harder at what they share. It's to look for the one mark only one of them has: a hand that moves, a bird landing on top, the grain of the wood. What would tell these apart? On the first Nyaya day you met the chain that runs from false knowledge to pain, and the release that comes when false knowledge goes. Handled well, doubt stops one piece of false knowledge at the door. Rush it, and you call the post a person and run, or call the person a post and walk past someone who needed help. Stay with it honestly, and one small thing gets seen as it is. For Nyaya, that small seeing belongs to the same work that ends in apavarga, release. Tomorrow, a close neighbor asks not how we know, but what there is to know.
screen: `SAMSHAYA: DOUBT STARTS THE SEARCH.` · `DOUBT COMES RIGHT AFTER KNOWING.` · `LOOK FOR WHAT TELLS THEM APART.` · `APAVARGA: RELEASE.` · then, large: `WHAT WOULD TELL THESE APART?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you honestly don't know yet, and don't rush to call it post or person. Notice what the two possibilities share and what would tell them apart; when the mind grabs at an answer, come back to the breath. If you pray, you can hold the question before God and simply wait.
Nyaya. Today, samshaya, doubt: the mind caught between two, where honest inquiry begins, on a path that aims at release.
Your line: Nyaya, logic. Honest doubt is a doorway, not a failure. That's today, done.

1166.title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
1166.hook: a school that wants to list everything there is opens its book with one word you wouldn't expect: dharma
1166.howItsDone: Vaisheshika is studied in traditional Sanskrit schools alongside Nyaya, often as one joined system, through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries.

segments.voice: Yesterday Nyaya ended at dusk: the post or the person, and doubt as the doorway to a search that ends in release. A second school opens today.
screen: `NYAYA: FROM DOUBT TO RELEASE.` · `A NEW SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: A sack of rice has split on the kitchen floor. Grains under the stove, in the corners, between the tiles. You crouch and start picking them up, one by one, and a strange thought arrives: this whole sack, this whole meal, is only ever grains. There's a story people tell about the sage who founded today's school: his name, Kanada, came from living on grains, gleaned one by one from harvested fields. Whether or not that's history, it fits. His school would go on to say the world itself is made of tiny grains.
screen: `RICE ON THE KITCHEN FLOOR.` → `ONLY EVER GRAINS.` → `KANADA, THE GRAIN-GATHERER.`

segments.voice: The school is Vaisheshika, and its root text is the Vaisheshika Sutra, credited to Kanada. You might expect it to open with matter. It doesn't. Its first sutra says, in effect: now, therefore, we will explain dharma. The next says what dharma is: that from which come both rising up in this world and the highest good. So before a single atom appears, the school says why it's counting at all. Knowing what the world is made of, and how things really differ, is meant to serve a good life and, finally, freedom. That's the note Nyaya struck, and the two are close neighbors. Later thinkers joined them, so you'll often hear Nyaya-Vaisheshika: one asking how we know, the other asking what there is to know. Then the name. Tradition links Vaisheshika to vishesha, particularity: what makes one thing this one and not that one. Later teachers of the school took it all the way down: two of the tiniest particles of earth, alike in every quality, still aren't copies, and vishesha keeps each one itself. The atoms come tomorrow. But notice the starting point. Not that everything is one blur, but that everything is particular. Carried out of the classroom, that turns tender. The grain on the floor, the stranger on the bus, the person who annoys you: each is really itself, not interchangeable. A school of atoms that begins with dharma refuses to let anything be just another one.
screen: `THE SUTRA OF KANADA.` · `IT OPENS WITH DHARMA.` · `A NEIGHBOR TO NYAYA.` · `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · then, large: `NOTHING IS JUST ANOTHER ONE.`

segments.voice: Pick something small near you, a grain of rice, a button, a leaf, and look at it as if it were the only one: its exact edge, its color in this light, the tiny mark no other has. Then, if you like, let one person come to mind and see them the same way, not a type, but this one. If you pray, you can give thanks for this one thing, exactly as it is.
Vaisheshika. The school of Kanada, linked by tradition to vishesha, particularity, and known for its atoms. Its sutra opens with dharma.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. In this school, nothing is just another one. See you tomorrow.

1167.title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
1167.hook: a kid tears a page in half, and in half again, and Vaisheshika asks where the tearing has to stop
1167.howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the teaching on atoms through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries, usually alongside Nyaya, as part of traditional Sanskrit study.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika, the school of Kanada, opened with dharma and with vishesha: each thing is itself. Now, the atoms.
screen: `VISHESHA: EACH THING IS ITSELF.` · `NOW, THE ATOMS.`

segments.voice: A kid at the kitchen table has a sheet of paper and a serious expression. She tears it in half. Then one half in half. Then that half. The pieces get smaller and her fingers clumsier, until she's pinching a scrap you can barely see. "Can I keep going?" she asks. "Forever?" The grown-up across the table just shrugs. Vaisheshika had an answer. Not forever. Somewhere down there the tearing has to stop, at something so small it has no halves left to tear. The school gave that something a name, and the name became the idea the school is known for.
screen: `TEARING A PAGE IN HALF.` → `CAN I KEEP GOING FOREVER?` → `NO: THE TEARING STOPS.`

segments.voice: The name is paramanu, often translated atom: the smallest of the small. A paramanu has no parts, so it can't come apart, and Vaisheshika calls it eternal: it can't be made and it can't be destroyed. You can't see one, either. So why believe in it? The school's thinkers gave an argument. If you could divide forever, a mountain would have endless parts, and so would a mustard seed. Then what makes the mountain bigger? So the dividing must stop somewhere, at a partless thing. That's an inference, the kind of step Nyaya says out loud. In the classic account the commentators give, atoms join in a ladder. Two atoms pair up. Then pairs gather, and you reach the smallest thing an eye can see: a speck of dust floating in a beam of sunlight. From there, upward, to clay and rivers and mountains. There are atoms of earth, of water, of fire, of air, each kind carrying its own qualities. Everything you can see is made of parts. Everything made of parts, sooner or later, comes apart: the cup, the house, the body. But what it's made of doesn't vanish. The pieces go back down the ladder and wait. That's an unusual kind of comfort. Vaisheshika doesn't say nothing is lost. It says the breaking happens in the joints, not at the bottom of things.
screen: `PARAMANU: THE SMALLEST OF THE SMALL.` · `NO PARTS, SO IT NEVER COMES APART.` · `A MOUNTAIN AND A MUSTARD SEED.` · `A SPECK IN A SUNBEAM.` · then, large: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.`

segments.voice: Let your attention move through your body as an assembly of parts: hands, shoulders, the back against the chair, the feet on the floor. Then hold one thing that has come apart lately, a plan, a routine, maybe something more, without fixing it, and notice that what it was made of, the effort, the care, the time, hasn't simply disappeared. If you pray, you can rest in what you trust does not come apart.
Vaisheshika. The school of particulars and of the paramanu: the partless smallest thing, which never comes apart, where all dividing has to stop.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. What things are made of goes back down the ladder and waits. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1168.title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
1168.hook: a red mango falls from a tree, and Vaisheshika finds six different kinds of thing in that one moment
1168.howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn its list of categories, the padarthas, at the start of their study, and later Nyaya-Vaisheshika primers teach the list with absence added as a seventh.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaisheshika, the atoms: the paramanu, partless, so it never comes apart, and the breaking that happens in the joints.
screen: `THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.` · `SIX KINDS OF THING.`

segments.voice: A ripe mango lets go of its branch and drops into the grass. Thud. Less than a second. Ask what happened, and the answer seems simple: a mango fell. Vaisheshika would gently disagree. In that one second, it would say, you were looking at several different kinds of thing, braided so tightly you never noticed the seams. There's the mango. There's its red. There's the falling. And a few quieter ones you'd only spot if someone pointed. Today Vaisheshika points.
screen: `A MANGO FALLS. THUD.` → `ONE EVENT?` → `SEVERAL KINDS OF THING, BRAIDED.`

segments.voice: The Vaisheshika Sutra names its kinds of thing early on, and the word for them is padartha, which tradition explains as the meaning of a word. Anything that can be named and known is a padartha. The Sutra's list has six. Watch them in the mango. First, substance, dravya: the mango itself, which holds everything else. Second, quality, guna: its red, its sweetness, its weight. Third, action, karma: the falling. The same word as karma, but here it simply means motion. Fourth, the universal, samanya: mango-ness, what this mango shares with every other, so one word can name them all. Fifth, particularity, vishesha, the word tradition links to the school's name: what makes this mango, at the very bottom, not that one. And sixth, inherence, samavaya: the glue. The red doesn't sit beside the mango like a sticker. It's in it, belonging. Later writers in the school added a seventh: absence. The mango no longer on the branch. The empty place is real too. So Vaisheshika isn't making the world complicated. It's teaching you to see the seams. At home, that turns out to be useful. Someone you love snaps at you. The person is the substance. The irritation is a quality, and it comes and goes. The snapping is an action, and it's over. When you can tell them apart, the snap doesn't have to become the whole person.
screen: `PADARTHA: WHAT A WORD CAN NAME.` · `SUBSTANCE, QUALITY, ACTION.` · `UNIVERSAL, PARTICULAR, INHERENCE.` · `LATER, A SEVENTH: ABSENCE.` · then, large: `SEE THE SEAMS.`

segments.voice: Look at something in front of you, a cup, a plant, your own hand, and name the substance, one quality, and any action, even a small one. Then let someone who irritated you recently come to mind, and name the person, the mood and what they did, noticing how the mood and the action pass while the person stays. If you pray, you can hold that person, not their mood, before God.
Vaisheshika. A school that names the kinds of thing in the world: substance, quality, action, the universal, the particular, inherence, and later, absence.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. A person is more than a mood or a moment. See you tomorrow.

1169.title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
1169.hook: Vaisheshika's list of what the world is made of ends with two items that aren't stuff at all: the self, and a mind that can only hold one thing at a time
1169.howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the nine substances, from earth to mind, as part of the school's list of categories, and the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition uses the self's marks in its arguments that the self is real.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vaisheshika, six kinds of thing in one falling mango, and the habit of seeing the seams: the person, the mood, the action. Today closes a week.

You're on the phone, nodding along, and at the same time reading an email. Then the voice on the phone says, "So what do you think?" And there's a little gap. You heard every word. Or did you? The sound reached your ears. But something wasn't connecting. Vaisheshika had no phones, but it noticed that kind of gap, and used it as evidence: that gap, the school said, is how you know there's a mind. Today the school finishes its list of what the world is made of, and the last two items are you.
screen: `ON THE PHONE, READING EMAIL.` → `"SO WHAT DO YOU THINK?"` → `THE GAP IS EVIDENCE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's first category was substance, and the Vaisheshika Sutra names nine. Earth, water, fire, air: the four kinds of atom. Then akasha, the space that carries sound. Then time and direction, which let us say before and after, here and there. And last, two that aren't stuff at all: the self, atman, and the mind, manas. Start with the self. How do you know there is one? The Sutra lists its marks, and the first is breathing out and breathing in. Then the eyelids opening and closing, life itself, the movement of the mind, and pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort. Breath is a sign of the self. Now the mind. Sometimes, the Sutra notes, self, senses and object are all in contact, and still no knowing happens. The phone talked; you didn't take it in. Something has to be the gate, and that gate is the mind. In this school the mind is tiny, so it can join only one sense at a time. On this view, nobody truly reads the email and hears the call at once; the mind only switches, quickly, back and forth. So the week closes. Nyaya brought five steps said out loud, three kinds of talk, reasons that only look like reasons, and doubt as a doorway. Vaisheshika brought dharma at the start, the atoms, the seams. And at the end of its list, a breathing self and a mind that can only hold one thing at a time.
screen: `NINE SUBSTANCES.` · `BREATH IS A SIGN OF THE SELF.` · `THE MIND: ONE THING AT A TIME.` · `A WEEK OF NYAYA AND VAISHESHIKA.` · then, large: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes or lower your gaze, and stay with one thing: the breath going out and coming in, the first of the self's marks in the Sutra's list. When a sound pulls you away, that's the gate swinging; no problem, swing it back to the breath. If you pray, you can let each breath be offered, one at a time.
Vaisheshika. Its nine substances end with the self, known by signs like breathing, and the mind, a gate that lets in one thing at a time.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. The mind is one gate, for one thing at a time. A week of two schools, done.
